transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-04-22 15:00 UTC | Duration ~60m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood), Marco Diaz (LucidAI CTO), Sasha Ivanov (Lucid ML Eng), Emma Li (Lucid Infra), Nadia Park (Prod)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about an hour, quick intros, Priya will drive the tech portion, i'll handle pricing/security follow-ups.
[00:15] Marco: thanks, yeah, excited — quick context: we run a 7B LLM family for summarization and code assist, latency target is 150ms p95 on short prompts, and data residency is required so we are evaluating on-prem or VPC.
[00:30] Priya: cool, that helps. can you confirm model variant — is it a gpt-style transformer with 2048 context, per-token KV caching enabled?
[00:40] Sasha: correct, 2048, we keep KV cache warm for active sessions; most requests are ~40-80 tokens.
[00:50] Priya: great. agenda — we'll cover quantization options (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ), expected accuracy deltas, runtime implications for throughput/latency (kernels, batching), and deployment notes for VPC/on-prem.

[01:05] Priya: starting with accuracy: GPTQ is widely used for post-training quantization, tends to give good size reduction but sometimes has layer-wise outliers that cause hallucination-regression on narrow prompt sets. AWQ (the newer asymmetric weight quant) often preserves accuracy better on causal LLMs because it handles activation distributions differently.
[01:25] Sasha: what's the typical BLEU/ROUGE or classification delta we should expect on a 7B? we saw earlier PRs that mentioned 1-3% metric drop?
[01:35] Priya: yes, on average GPTQ may have 1-4% drop depending on dataset and calibration; AWQ has shown sub-1% in many workloads but it depends — for code models or models with lots of numerical tokens, GPTQ can introduce tokenization artifacts.
[01:50] Marco: and INT8 versus FP8 — are we talking about activations being quantized too or weights only?
[02:00] Priya: good question. INT8 typically refers to integer 8-bit for both weights and activations in many runtimes; pure weight-only quant (like some GPTQ flows) keeps activations in fp16 to reduce accuracy loss. FP8 is an emerging option (E4M3/E5M2 variants) that keeps dynamic range for activations and often gives better numeric fidelity than INT8 while still improving throughput. runtime support for FP8 is spotty — some kernels support it natively on newer GPUs and Triton kernels, but it's not universal.
[02:25] Luis (interject): also workload matters for latency — FP8 may reduce compute but memory bandwidth and kernel dispatch overhead could dominate for short sequences.

[02:40] [03:00] Priya: runtime notes — Redwood runtime picks kernels per model shape and seq-length. For your 40-80 token typical requests, continuous batching and token-level batching help. But quantized kernels often have different batching sweet spots — INT8 kernels may use faster GEMM paths but need quant/dequant steps that add per-batch overhead.
[03:20] Emma: how does KV cache behave with quantized models? we worry about memory footprint on on-prem servers.
[03:30] Priya: KV cache is largely orthogonal to weight quantization — keys and values are activations and stored in fp16 or bf16 in most implementations. But if you quantize activations to INT8 or use FP8, you can reduce KV cache size, though that requires runtime support and careful attention to accumulation precision. More commonly, weight quant reduces model size on disk and VRAM for weights, but KV memory is still a big portion of runtime RAM for long contexts. for 2048 with many concurrent sessions, KV dominates.
[03:55] Sasha: ok, so for our workload KV will still take majority of the memory, quantizing weights alone won't fix concurrency limits.
[04:05] Priya: correct. you can combine model sharding and aggressive batching to amortize KV overhead, or use prefix/KV caching so idle sessions don't keep full KV in GPU memory. Redwood supports prefix eviction and on-demand warming.

[04:30] [05:00] Marco: what's the expected latency tradeoff if we go INT8 GPTQ vs AWQ fp8-like? will p95 change a lot?
[05:10] Priya: empirically for 7B we see INT8 GPTQ reduce model load and sometimes token latency by 10-25% on throughput-heavy workloads. AWQ with FP8-like behavior can be similar or slightly better on quality but kernel maturity matters. p95 can be sensitive to cold starts: quantized kernels sometimes have longer first-inference due to conversion steps; subsequent tokens are faster. Also batching matters — with small batch sizes p95 could be higher if quant overhead isn't amortized.
[05:40] Jordan: also note CPU-to-GPU transfer, pinned memory, and kernel launch overhead. For latency SLO you may want dedicated pools at the cost of utilization.

[05:55] [06:30] Priya: about accuracy regression debugging — we recommend a small eval harness: 200-500 prompts reflecting your user flows, run baseline fp16 (or fp32) and each quant method, compute token-level and semantic metrics, and inspect hallucination cases. GPTQ can have catastrophic per-layer errors; we use per-layer emulation to find and rehose problematic layers (e.g., re-run those layers at fp16).
[06:55] Sasha: is that something Redwood can run for us or we need to bring infra?
[07:05] Priya: we can run the bench in Redwood Dedicated or in your on-prem env if you share binaries and a small sample. preferred is to run with your exact tokenizer and prompt-set to get realistic numbers.

[07:20] [07:45] Marco: on security/regulatory — we need KMS support and audit logs, and can't have model artifacts leaving our VPC.
[07:50] Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer KMS integration and private control plane; we can also run an air-gapped on-prem package. we'll send the security pack and SOC2/ISO docs after.

[08:05] Priya: deployment notes — on-prem GPUs — which hardware are you targeting? A100 80GB? H100?
[08:15] Emma: we have A100 40GB and a few 80GB on prem; considering adding H100 next quarter.
[08:20] Priya: good. A100 memory constraints mean model sharding + quantization helps; 40GB devices are tight for 7B with large KV concurrency. H100 gives better FP8 support and faster kernels for some quant methods.

[08:40] [09:00] Luis: small kernel note — some open-source AWQ/GPTQ implementations use CPU pre/post processing steps that block async GPU queues; Redwood's runtime avoids blocking by overlapping quant convert ops but that requires integration.

[09:15] Priya: practical recommendation for LucidAI: 1) run GPTQ and AWQ on your 7B dev set to measure accuracy deltas, 2) test runtime p95 with your typical batch size and sequence lengths on A100 40GB, 3) consider hybrid approach: weight-quantize with GPTQ but keep a few sensitive layers at fp16 to avoid regression, 4) evaluate FP8 on H100 when available.

[09:45] Sasha: about hybrid — how many layers typically need to stay fp16?
[09:55] Priya: depends; many customers keep 2-4 top attention layers fp16 — often the final MLP or attention output layers show sensitivity. it's empirical.

[10:10] Marco: for benchmarking, we also want throughput numbers at 95th token latency and cost delta estimates.
[10:15] Jordan: we'll provide spreadsheet with estimated tokens/sec, p95, and cost per 1M tokens for hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem amortized.

[10:30] [11:00] Priya: one more gotcha — quantization can change cache warm-up behavior. With different kernel ordering we sometimes see slightly different token distributions which interact with your prefix caching; we'll include prefix-warmup tests in the bench.

[11:15] Marco: sounds good. any blockers we should know?
[11:20] Priya: mainly access to a representative prompt set and a dev VM or sample artifacts. plus confirmation of target hardware so we can match kernels.

[11:35] Jordan: recap and next steps — Priya will run GPTQ vs AWQ bench and upload results, Marco will provide prompt-set and success criteria, Jordan will send pricing and security docs and scheduling link for an on-prem pilot. we'll reconvene after bench results.

[11:50] Marco: thanks everyone. small note — we also want to see memory breakdown (weights vs KV vs activation) per concurrency level.
[12:00] Priya: noted, we'll include memory breakdown charts.

[12:15] Jordan: okay thanks all, meeting ended.

Notes: transcript contains small transcription errors and occasional speaker mis-attribution; timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/gptq-lucidai (bench spreadsheet), https://redwood.ai/security/lucidai-pack (security pack link).
